metadata.title: Nobody Has Built This Yet
metadata.author: Amos Jaimes
metadata.note: Explains what the plan WILL do — the pipeline, the corpus contract, the model it feeds, and the gate that decides whether any of it proceeds. Nothing in the plan has been executed: all 73 steps are unchecked. No code was run and no source data was read while making this reel. Every number on screen is a design parameter chosen in the plan, never a measured outcome — the reel says so explicitly in the opening and closing beats.

metadata.claims_discipline: Design parameters stated as decisions, not results: the 1001-point grid, the 0.999 similarity threshold, the 150,000-spectrum gate. The novelty claim ('nobody has built this yet') is voiced as the project's own position, not as a literature finding — the plan cites no survey. B05 is labelled schematic on screen and reads no source data.

beats.narration_text: A foundation model is one network pretrained on a large pile of unlabelled data, then adapted to specific tasks with very little labelled data. Text has them. Images have them. Raman spectroscopy does not. So the question is not whether that would be useful. It is what the pretraining data would have to look like before the result could be trusted.

props.command: I want to pretrain one model on pooled public Raman spectra, then adapt it to my own labelled tasks. Before any training: specify the corpus. What has to be true of it for the downstream numbers to mean anything?
output: Start with the corpus contract, not the architecture.

beats.narration_text: This is a plan, not a result. Nothing in it has been run yet — no data downloaded, no corpus built, no model trained. What follows is the specification: what will be assembled, in what order, and the one gate that decides whether the next stage is allowed to begin at all.

props.text:
This is the plan,
before any of it runs.

No corpus yet.
No model yet.
Just the contract.

beats.narration_text: Every spectrum that enters has to be made comparable first, and the rules are fixed in advance rather than decided per source. One shared axis: a thousand and one points, from three fifty to eighteen fifty wavenumbers, at a step of one point five. Clean the axis, remove cosmic ray spikes, resample, then scale each spectrum using only its valid points. And no baseline correction anywhere — that step cost eight points of accuracy last time it was measured here.

Then the build itself, and every stage in it exists to throw something away. Harmonise onto the shared grid. Drop spectra with too few valid points to be worth anything. Remove any copy of the evaluation data. Cap sources that would otherwise flood the corpus from a single map. Remove near-identical twins. Split by sample. Write the result with a manifest recording what each stage removed, so the losses are auditable rather than invisible.

props.title: Every stage removes something
props.caption: The manifest records what each stage dropped.

beats.narration_text: Harmonising deserves a closer look, because it is where most pooled datasets quietly go wrong. Sources do not share an axis. One instrument covers part of the range, another covers a different part. The tempting fix is to stretch each source to fill the grid. This plan refuses that. Wherever a source has no measurement, the grid holds zero and carries a mask saying so. The model is told what is missing instead of being handed an invention.

The stage that matters most is the leakage guard. The downstream evaluation uses a labelled bacteria dataset, and that same data circulates publicly — inside at least one collection being pooled here. If a copy reaches pretraining, the model has seen the answers before the exam, and every number after it is inflated by an unknown amount. So the guard runs twice.

lines: If a copy lands in pretraining,
meta: caught two ways: exact match, and near-duplicate

beats.narration_text: And then a gate, written before anyone knows whether it will pass. The audit reads the manifest and counts the usable pretraining spectra that survived every filter. If that number clears one hundred and fifty thousand, the model stage is allowed to begin. If it does not, the plan says to stop and reconsider the sources — not to lower the threshold. Deciding that in advance is the only way the number means anything.

lines: Written down before the build runs,
so it cannot be moved afterwards.
meta: the threshold is a decision, not yet an outcome

beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you are assembling a pretraining corpus from public sources and you plan to evaluate on a public benchmark, the first thing to establish is whether your benchmark is already inside your corpus. Here is a prompt for that. Ask it before you train anything, because afterwards you cannot tell the difference.

props.command: I am pooling public datasets to pretrain on, and I will evaluate on a public benchmark. List the ways that benchmark could already be inside my corpus — redistributions, renamed copies, rescaled or resampled versions — and how I would detect each one.

beats.narration_text: Nobody has built this yet. Working notes from a Humanitarians AI fellowship — the failures are the part worth keeping.
